utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we start with the witness, I think there's a procedural matter that we have to deal with. And yesterday Mr. Karnavas promised me to have some feedback concerning one witness. Mr. Karnavas, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I apologise for -- thank you, Your Honour, and thank you for giving us the extra time to make a more comprehensive argument, though I must say getting ready for Mr. Deronjic, my argument is going to be crude and perhaps not as eloquent as I would like it to be. In any event, if I can work backwards with respect to the pleadings with this particular witness. The Prosecution on 5 December, 2003, filed a motion and attached to the motion in the very last page with respect to this particular witness, it notes that her testimony, and I quote here: "Does not relate to any elements of the crimes charged." And then it states: "In view of this and in the interest of expedience and efficiency, the Prosecution submits that this witness's testimony should be admitted under 92 bis with no cross-examination." So that was the very latest that we heard from the Prosecution. Then if we were to go, for instance, to the Prosecutor's notice -- the summary of the witnesses. On page 32, it would be paragraph 78. This was a motion that was filed or a pleading that was filed on 4 November, 2003, titled Prosecution's notice for filing revised witness list and motion to remove additional witnesses from witness list. And I quote with respect to this particular witness the Prosecution states there in a somewhat contradictory form to what we just heard: "This evidence is relevant to all paragraphs and all counts of the indictment." That's paragraph 78, page 32 of that particular motion. Then if you were to go, Your Honours, to 8 November, 2002, to the Prosecution's -- this was filed under seal. The Prosecution's filing of amended pre-trial brief pursuant to Rule 65 ter and list of exhibits pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E)(v) [sic]. On page 78, there is an argument with respect to the issue of genocide. I don't want to go into it, but nonetheless I think it can be found on paragraph 203 on page 78 -- I mean, 85. And if you look at that paragraph and the following paragraph, it talks about the particular argument that the Prosecution wishes to put forward with respect to the issue of genocide. Lastly, I was -- we were in a bit of a rush, but nonetheless we did manage to look at the trial testimony of this particular witness during the Krstic trial. And there was a very pointed question that was put by Judge Riad who was the President of the Trial Chamber at that time. And I'm quoting from page 5.855 where Judge Riad says, and this, it begins on line 21, Ms., Ms. -- I can't pronounce the name: "In fact my question is based on some of the answers you gave to my colleagues, my very eminent Judge colleagues which touch on a very basic problem, a very basic issue and this is the planning for the future and the continuation of life for this community because some communities could not rise up again after destruction and history. Some continents even." And it goes on. And the answer to that question that was posed, which can be found on page 5.857, and I'm quoting from line 4, this is her answer: "I think that would be a very interesting to see in what way the role of the woman will change in these patriarchal Islamic families. This concerns the rule areas to a greater extent because in-town women have their jobs, their professions, and they are unable to live on their own." And it goes on and on. Now, I think given the answer where she says, "It would be interesting to see in what way," we have as part of our preparation and defence for Mr. Blagojevic, we have begun to look into this issue. And we do know that there are some statistics that are being gathered by the international community, and I believe we are hoping to have some more concrete figures perhaps from the office of the high representative which is currently working in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, naturally these statistics would go to the returnees and the return of abandoned property. That's not an exact scientific measure, because at least in my experience and having worked for OHR in Bosnia, it seems that many refugees or displaced persons would prefer to sell their properties as to -- versus returning to their village or their town. But nonetheless, there is a mechanism for them to get their property back and have the option to live wherever they wish to live pursuant to the constitution of the BiH. The statistics show, and I don't want to be nailed down on this, but it's my understanding and I say this as an officer of the court, that the statistics so far show that perhaps we are in a figure of 90 per cent. Now I will try to get more concrete figures. And the expectation is that within some point there will be 100 per cent returnees to the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's one measuring stick. The other measuring stick, I think, for this particular witness is given her own answer in this particular case, I think it would be vital to have her and I would suggest to the Prosecution that perhaps they could ask her to do some updated research because she's not polemical in her testimony. She's not -- and when I say polemical she's not hostile. She's not -- she doesn't seem to be taking a subjective position so -- and that's welcoming. And I think it might be worth for the Prosecution to ask her to do an updated survey, an updated report. But I do think, I do think, that her testimony is vital in this case. She is a psychologist. I think this was a vital question that was posed in the Krstic case. I think it remains a vital issue in this case. It goes to the heart of the issue of genocide. I think that the Prosecution initially had asserted that her testimony goes to all counts of the entire indictment. They then modified it. I don't know why. I suspect they have good reasons. But nonetheless I would request that she be brought in. I don't think that her entire testimony would take more than a day, a day and a half at most. So I hope, you know, my long-winded explanation, as a result of lack of preparation, is sufficient to answer this particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is there any response from the Prosecution? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The last thing Mr. Karnavas had read about the -- it didn't have anything to do with the elements is -- I'm not sure what that was based on and that is not correct. This testimony is -- was placed before the Krstic Court and this Court to show the impact on the victims of the female community, the surviving -- some of the surviving males and females. This witness had treated and interviewed many, many Srebrenica women, and she was basically testifying about the abject misery of the community as victim impact evidence, which we, as you know, since we do not have sentencing hearings in this case, it's incumbent upon the Prosecution to put on any victim impact evidence that it has in its case in-chief. Now, as this evidence came on in -- as victim impact in the Krstic trial, it was also evident that the -- as the Court reviewed whether or not Muslims in Eastern Bosnia had suffered destruction or part destruction, they looked as you can tell from the questions of the Judge and from the arguments into whether or not the evidence she provided was evidence of the -- relating to the destruction of the group. So that is another point that we would like the Court to look at. She has testified in Krstic. She has been fully cross-examined in Krstic. Nothing she says goes to the acts or conducts of this accused. She really testifies about the misery and the living conditions and the horror that the people who survived this without their men have lived there. That will not change. It is difficult for her to testify on these subjects. It's difficult for her to come back. She will not fundamentally change her perspective on that, I am sure. And she does not provide any statistics or any survey or anything like that. She's just talked to the women and she's seen where they lived, and she told the Court about it. This is precisely the kind of evidence that 92 bis is most appropriate for. It would be difficult for her to come back and have to relive the nightmare of the women that she has spoken to. And, so we would request this Court to consider 92 bis and allow her Krstic testimony to come in. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very, very brief response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very brief, Your Honour. Very brief. First, I was quoting from the pleadings that were submitted by the Prosecutor. I quoted verbatim. The first quote came from tab A of their motion. So I don't think I'm out of line on that. Secondly, victim impact is an element in genocide, not just for sentencing but also in whether the atrocities and the crimes were of such nature that we can say that there was a permanent effect on the community, either in part or in whole. Thirdly, there was no cross-examination of this witness in the Krstic case, so there was no confrontation. I don't know what the reasons were. They obviously have their own tactics. Fourthly, they brought her in in essence as an expert, as an expert psychologist. So she was not just an observer, an eyewitness or a survivor. She was an expert. Naturally, she was doing that as part of her job. So she placed herself into that nightmarish situation, because that's part of her job, just as a physician places himself in a hospital to deal with individuals that are in a dying -- are in dying conditions. Somebody has to do that work. I think I would agree that it's traumatic to testify regarding these events, but nonetheless we have certain rights in this case. And I don't think that Mr. McCloskey's argument is very persuasive at all. I do think it's necessary for her to come in and testify. If she doesn't want to testify, then she should not -- then this Court should not accept her testimony at all, period. End of story. They can find somebody else. If the Prosecutor, if the Prosecutor, is saying today that she is unavailable for cross-examination, then she's unavailable for direct examination, Your Honour. That's the way it should work, because we have rights as well. And he hasn't -- and Mr. Blagojevic hasn't been convicted. And so he's saying this is for sentencing purposes; and I'm saying, well, if you're going to use this for sentencing purposes, let us cross-examine. She should have more data. If her own answers are that, it would be interesting to see. She's had more time. So I don't think the Prosecutor should get a freebie on this one. They get to put on evidence and we don't get to. Because I'm still left with the option of calling her as my own witness. I find it -- I don't want to notch it up at this level, but I find it supremely ironic that one month they say that she goes -- she's involved in the entire indictment, and then later when it suits them, well, nema problema, we don't need to have her. Not important. Which one is it, Your Honour? And again I don't mean to get confrontational on this, but I think either she's in or she's out, not half way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after the consultations with my colleagues and after hearing the submissions from both parties, we believe that this witness is indeed a victim impact witness. And we go through her testimony in another case. It is true that nothing she says goes to the acts and the conducts of the accused in this case, the Blagojevic case. As for the matter of the genocide, pending the decisions of the Appeals Chamber on another case, at this moment we would like to say that the genocide happened during the Srebrenica incidents. But this is not the question in our case. In our case we have to find out the linkage between the genocide and Mr. Karnavas's client, the accused. This is the most important matter. As for the filings of the Prosecution, we believe that we should rely on the latest filings from the Prosecution, because along with the proceedings of this case both parties as well as the Bench could have a better understanding of the case. So at this stage, we will not make a decision whether to hear this witness live or admit his testimony or statement into the evidence. We would like to ask the Defence counsel to submit whatever their objections or concrete reasons for the cross-examination in the written form. This witness could be a rebuttal witness in the future but not now. At this moment, we are not going to make any decisions concerning this matter. It is so decided. Well, having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could pick up where we left off yesterday. Yesterday I believe we were discussing the issue of the declaration that was signed by the representatives of the Muslim community and by you back on 17 July 1995. Do you recall that's where we left off?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you had the opportunity to review your records overnight and perhaps even look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, this document was introduced by the Prosecution in two versions, 36.1 and 36.2/A. I believe the Prosecution's official translated version was 36.2/A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe yesterday we were discussing whether this document represented a true reflection of the situation as it was occurring and as it had occurred between July 12th, 1995, and July 17, 1995. And if I'm not mistaken, it was your understanding that this was a truthful representation of the situation. Do you still maintain that or was I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think that this was the question where we broke off yesterday. I wanted to have a look at the transcript with respect to this question. The way you posed your question implied that you believed that this document was not accurate. And I said no, which means, since you were discussing the issue of semantics, you must be aware of the fact that I am also aware of the broader issue. And you were implying that I believed that the entire document was not accurate. Which is what I indicated yesterday. I do not have any other answer to provide at this point. I let you finish your point, your argument, and it was my intention to give a comment on the issue once you've completed your argument. In my statement before the Prosecutor, which has been recorded, I asked -- I was asked whether the document was entirely truthful, and I denied it and said, no, which means that certain portions of the document were accurate and others were not. I made a note in the original transcript, which is much broader than the summarised version that the Court has, the part where I mention this particular document, and if you want me to, I can read out the exact wording of the question and my answer. And this other document in the summarised version, the redacted version, I also made a note of the exact part of the document where the issue is discussed. Now, I don't want to waste your time on reading the document, but the issue was whether the statement that Muslims were able to remain in Srebrenica, that they could choose whether to stay or to leave, whether this statement would be considered to be truthful and whether it corresponded to the situation as it was on the ground. And I responded to the question, I said that my opinion is and was at the time that this was not possible, that it was my belief that Muslims could not remain in Srebrenica, even if they had expressed such a wish because the actual circumstances did not allow for that possibility. And I went on to enumerate the reasons that made this option impossible. It is true that on the meeting of the 12th, I did offer this possibility pursuant to the order of President Karadzic. I spelled it out. It was within those three options that the president wanted me to convey to the Muslim representatives at the Fontana Hotel. So I did mention this particular option, but I believed that due to the circumstances on the ground after the takeover of Srebrenica by the members of the Serbian army did not allow for the possibility of Muslims to remain in Srebrenica. I did not question the entire wording of the document when I said that. The document also contains the issue of transport of civilians, women and children, from Potocari and the way it was carried out, escorted by UNPROFOR and the police and so on and so forth. And we agreed, all the three parties, that this was -- this transport was done in a correct manner, in light of the circumstances as they were at the time. So I did not comment on the entirety of the document. In response to the question dealing with segments of this document, I said that they were not accurate. Likewise, I indicated that the document did not contain all of the events taking place at the time. I drafted it with the purpose of having a confirmation of what was my responsibility, namely the transport of the civilians. I agree that it should have been dealt with more extensively. And it is true that on the 17th I was already familiar with some of the crimes that had taken place, the Kravica incident, but I did not believe it to be necessary to be part of this document. So therefore, you were hasty in your conclusion that I consider the entire document to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you finished, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I notice that you have in front of you in tabs your prior testimony from previous hearings. So I take it you had a chance to review what you said so you could be correct today. Mr. Deronjic --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I apologise, really. This is my last testimony. I don't have any of my other previous statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Deronjic, before we get to this document, you indicate -- let's talk about one issue that you raised on your own. It wasn't part of my question, we were going to get to it, but you raised it nonetheless and let's deal with it at this point. And that is the issue of whether -- had the Muslims expressed an interest to remain in Srebrenica, whether that was feasible, given the circumstances. And I understand your answer is, no, that was not feasible. Now, am I -- are we correct in assuming that one of the reasons that wasn't feasible was because it would have been difficult, if not impossible, to provide security for those Muslims during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That is one of the reasons why I believed this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they had left Srebrenica, it would have also been rather difficult to move them back into Srebrenica and provide them protection while at the same time keeping out the Muslim military, which the UN apparently was reluctant or unable or unwilling to do pursuant to their mandate as it was required by them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are assertions. I don't know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well -- okay. Let's not play games. Srebrenica, before it fell, was it demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the information that I have - and I'm not an expert; I never seriously dealt with it - but military information states that Srebrenica was not completely demilitarised. And of course there certain evidence of that also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know for a fact that it wasn't demilitarised, Mr. Deronjic. You were the number one person for Karadzic on the ground, and you had access to information. So you know for a fact that it wasn't demilitarised. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said that I did not directly deal with that. I didn't any contacts with UNPROFOR during their stay in Srebrenica, no contact at all. But I did hear from military sources that Srebrenica was not demilitarised. And I could establish that also, based on the fact that Muslims very frequently carried out military actions from that allegedly demilitarised zone. So are you satisfied with the answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it it was a rumour that you heard. You had no real substantial basis for that; it was just a rumour. Because that's an absurdity if that's what you're alleging right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This is argumentive, Your Honour. And we'll just go downhill from there. It's not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the last paragraph of this document. Now, in the last paragraph it indicates that: "No incidents were provoked by any side during the evacuation and the Serbian side observed all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the international law of war." You put that statement in there, did you not, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote the text, with the help of a Judge. I explained that, but I authored the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made sure that that paragraph was in there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because it was important, at least to show to the international community, that your evacuation process - since you had been tasked with that by President Karadzic - had been conducted in a lawful manner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was important for me that I have that assurance or confirmation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then at some point the Dutch representatives insisted on inserting a certain text with that. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's leave aside what the Dutch have inserted. Could you verify for us whether that statement that you insisted on putting in and that we now know was drafted with the assistance of a trained jurist, was that truthful? Yes or no will do, but then you can give your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can be no answer like that, just like that. Partially it is true, otherwise in another part it's not. Please, Mr. Karnavas, how is it possible to respond to such a question with a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you said "partially." Tell me which part is correct.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to look at the document, then I can quote so that I don't have to just speak off the top of my head. I said that -- I told you which part was incorrect, and that was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I'm looking at the last paragraph. We can put it on the ELMO. We also have a copy in Serbian, and I know that you read English as well. So -- now I'm just focusing on that last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about this part after the agreement was concluded, the civilian population -- is that what you're talking about, the evacuation of the Srebrenica population was conducted correctly and everything that we had agreed on in relation to the evacuation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not see the original of the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just -- I don't want to go over every inch of this document. I just want to go over the last paragraph. The last paragraph, the very last paragraph reads, and you can follow along with me. "No incidents were provoked by any side during the evacuation and the Serbian side observed all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the International Law of War." And then other -- some text was also injected in there by the Dutch which said: "As far as the convoys escorted by UN forces were concerned."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There is another exhibit that has that written in there. The one on the ELMO doesn't have that. So if he's going to be questioned on that, it would be better to have the full, proper text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe we provided all of the documents. I have an extra copy in Srpski if you would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you've looked at this document, correct, recently?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would suspect you even looked at it last night, knowing you were going to be questioned first thing in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have it with me. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could look at the very last paragraph; look at it, read it, study it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier I asked you a question with respect to this paragraph, and I asked for a yes or no answer. And you indicated that it was very difficult because part of it is true, part of it is false or incorrect, however you wish to characterise it. So which part of this paragraph do you find to be truthful? And then, I guess by process of elimination, we can determine that the rest obviously is either false or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First in your previous question you asked about the complete document, what do I think. And I think that could be correct of you to say that. Secondly, as far as this paragraph is concerned, if I can talk about it in its entirety, and I will tell you it is not correct. Because those convoys that were leaving for Kladanj, people were being separated, even though this was an order of President Karadzic, his order related to the people about whom our intelligence services had information that they had committed war crimes. And we know today that this separation of people was systematic, meaning that all the men were taken from the convoys. And we know of their fate later. That is why this paragraph is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you suggesting today that at that time you were unaware of the separation and that it is only now, after the fact, that you have concluded that this paragraph, which you had special assistance of a jurist help you draft and inject the Geneva Conventions in there, are you suggesting that it was only after the fact that you realised that this was wrong and incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked the question whether I knew about this separation at the time. I did know and I did react about that, and I said that in all of my reports and I said through whom I reacted as well. What I did not know is I did not know the scale of this separation and the manner in which this was done. In the last days, when I was giving my statement, I wasn't aware whether all the men were separated or not. But I was provided with a lot of evidence that all men were separated from the convoys. I know about some of the fates of those people; for the others I don't know, but I know what was happening with them. And this convinced me that this part was not correct. At the time when I was drafting this document, I did know about certain separations, but I did not know whether it was systematic or not systematic or whether this was done on the recommendations of the president or whether these people were separated in some other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me be concrete. When you were drafting this paragraph, is it not a fact that you knew that this was false, that this was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not a correct interpretation. This was drafted on the 16th. On the 16th I did not have correct information about who was separated and how many people were separated, as well as the manner in which the separation was being carried out. What I know now is information that I got later. It was something that I compiled later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me jump ahead a little bit, and in timewise I'm going to go back. I'm jumping ahead in my cross. On the 13th, you met with Mr. Beara, right, you had contact with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, according to your testimony, Mr. Beara indicated that he was there to kill all of the Muslims that were there being warehoused in schools and in buses. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, how is it possible then on three days later when you draft this document, and how is it possible for you to stand here, after having taken an oath, and say that when you drafted this you thought that there had been no incidents and that everything that had been conducted was correct and lawful?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are constructing your own theories, and I agree with that; you are doing your job. But I will explain it to you very simply. On the 13th when Beara came to my office I said literally what he conveyed to me. You know how I acted; this is described in my interview. Up until that time in Bratunac, there was no systematic killing of people, except a major crime, an event, which happened in Kravica Oka about which I received an interpretation from Ljubisa Borovcanin and he told me what caused this massacre, how it took place, and what were the causes for all the consequences that occurred. On the 13th in the evening, or the 14th in the morning, prevented Mr. Beara from committing any kind of killings, even systematic ones in Bratunac. According to the instructions of Karadzic the way I interpreted it. The detainees were taken from Bratunac to Zvornik. So a large number of prisoners were alive on the 14th and they were transported to Zvornik. On the 14th in the morning, I went to see Karadzic - I think you will come to those questions - and I convoyed Mr. Beara's intentions the way he told them to Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic reacted, please allow me finish, you have stated a very large accusation. So allow me to explain that. Mr. Karadzic reacted the way he did and I got the impression he was going to do something, and I returned to Bratunac. I did not have any particular information over those few days from Zvornik. Of course some information was arriving and it was possible to conclude that some unforeseeable events were happening there, some things which were not foreseen in terms of killing people and so on. On the 16th, I drafted this document. I don't have complete information about what happened in Zvornik or Bratunac. So I'm telling you -- unless -- I did not have any information about any systematic murders nor did I know at the time that they had occurred. I went to the UNPROFOR base, aware that there had been some incidents, I had spoken about that. Aware that there had been some killings, I already had some information about the killings in the school, in the Konjevic Polje road and about this one at Kravica. So this document did not encompass those incidents, but the systematic killing and the fate of those people was not something that anybody had any information about. I don't know, I'm not claiming so, but I don't believe they were all killed on the 16th. I don't have information to that effect to this very day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, by your own admission today, by the 16th you had learned from Borovcanin, who was a close personal friend of yours, someone that was from Bratunac, albeit wasn't working in Bratunac but was there during that period of time, you had learned about the incident in Kravica that happened on the 13th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And I said that. You have that. That's already described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that not be an incident?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would that not be an incident? I don't understand what you're saying. It's a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It's a crime. Thank you. That was the -- I wanted you to fill in the blanks. So you knew of one particular crime. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also knew that there were other crimes, though you say you didn't know that they were "systematic." But nonetheless, those would be incidents, would they not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now -- at least with even your very limited knowledge which you claim to have had at that time, it would appear, it would appear, would it not, that this paragraph here, as was drafted by you with the help of a jurist, was utterly and completely false?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about limited knowledge, and you're talking about it in an ironic way. This is the only knowledge of it I had at the time, and these were the only incidents or crimes, whatever you like, which had taken place at that point in time. But that -- they do not reflect the essence of the tragedy which took place later. You know and we all know today that about 7.000 people were systematically killed. Are you claiming that this was happening in Bratunac in the same way this was happening in Zvornik. If you have that information, fine; but I don't have that information. So I knew that there were individual killings as well as major killings at the time when I was drafting the documents. But we're talking about the separation of men from the group of civilians in Potocari. In this paragraph, that should also be contained. And this is why I'm saying that this is not a correct document, or rather, the paragraph as part of this document is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just move on now, go back to the rest of your statement. We're still on 16th December 1997. So I'm going back to the same document that we were looking at yesterday, and that's D92/1 for identification purposes. That is your first encounter with the Office of the Prosecution. You were then asked -- you then indicate that the treatment of Muslims employed by UNPROFOR was also your job, and you say: "I was ordered by Radovan Karadzic that Muslims in the forces of UNPROFOR have amnesty and can go in any direction." Was that a truthful statement, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you granted them amnesty and you allowed them to go wherever they wished?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me at the UNPROFOR base what would be their fate. I called President Karadzic. We discussed it, and he said they could go freely wherever they wanted. And the majority of them, as far as I know, opted to go with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Further down in your statement you were asked about, from Mr. Ruez -- you were asked a question by Mr. Ralston. This is on paragraph 5. I don't have the exact -- paragraph 5, I believe, page 3. You were asked: "You say you escorted 10.000 of a population of 60 to 70.000 people from Srebrenica. What happened to the rest?" Then you give this rather convoluted answer, where you basically don't answer the question. Could you look at that and tell me whether your answer that you gave is correct. If you could just read it, and then we'll go over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Argumentative, Your Honour. It's unnecessary to throw-in adjectives of what he thinks of the answer. It's just going to create more problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could rephrase your question, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at the -- look at your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is that a truthful answer as far as what happened to the rest of those people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in possession of all of this information at that moment, and I think that what I said here is accurate. I was referring to the movement of the soldiers from Srebrenica towards Tuzla. I had information that elements of the Muslim army had surrendered to the Serbian army, elements managed to break through to Gorazde. The fact that I mentioned Ms. Rehn, this is also correct. At one point she paid a visit to her brother, I think it was in the autumn of 1995. And she expressly asked to be taken there and to learn how many people had been killed in the field. She wanted to see it for herself, and I personally was present in the field with her. So this information is also accurate. With your permission, I should like to comment the question of Mr. Ruez. He's talking about 50 to 60.000 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. If you could just answer my question, and if the Prosecutor wishes to ask you to expound on your answers with respect to Mr. Ruez, you'll have an opportunity. But my question here is directly: Are you stating that in 1997 -- as of 1997, you did not know about the massacres?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to clarify, which is some confusion that may add to the confusion. The JR in this particular interview is John Ralston. I think that maybe could cause some more confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested to know, Mr. Deronjic, that when you gave the statement back on December 16th, 1997, two years after the incidents in Srebrenica, as of that time you were still unaware of what had happened to all the people that had disappeared?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. I was aware of quite a few things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that there had been instances of systematic killings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So why -- may I ask, or why was it that you could just not tell him that I heard that they were systematically killed? Why not be straight instead of saying some fell in the hands of the Yugoslav army, there were -- others were fighting, and then go on about going to see the dead in the fields, and then asking the International Community to help dig up graves. Why go through all of that and not just say, you know what, there was a -- they were massacred, there were systematic killings, I wasn't involved. I heard about it. Why not say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to answer this question. Of course today you're talking about it in a courtroom and you are forgetting a simple fact that this took place in 1997. Today if I were to live in Bratunac with four children, I don't know if I would be able -- I would dare to say that. In particular in view of the circumstances at the time. I mean the general climate was hysterical when it came to the Tribunal. And this can still be felt in some parts of Yugoslavia Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the time to say that would mean to expose oneself to a great risk, a great danger. The Prime Minister Djindjic was assassinated by a group of people who were attempting to prevent, to obstruct cooperation with the Tribunal. And now you're asking me how it was that I did not say that in 1997. And yesterday I expressly told you that I had not said everything. Let me please finish. There is a much more important motive that I had in mind at the time, and that was to remain alive and for my family to remain alive, hoping and knowing that one day I would have an opportunity. Because as soon as I was summoned, I realised that I would have an opportunity to talk about these events in the manner that I described -- in the manner that I did in my last interview. Do you need more examples of that? I mean, yesterday I talked about it. I told you that I have been followed, that I had threats from various sides, that I had been warned directly as to what I should be saying. These are not just stories. I can provide hard evidence to support this. I'm not going to waste any more of your time for that. I will just state once again that for reasons of security, my own security, and the security of my family, I did not dare to address the most sensitive issue. And just one other thing. Not even today the government -- is the government of Republika Srpska capable or willing to investigate or to disclose the entire truth about Srebrenica. Not long ago, I read a report that was composed on behalf of Republika Srpska upon request of Mr. Petric [phoen] which report is full of misinformation and false --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you met with the Office of the Prosecution on February 4, 1998. You met with them on 21 October 1995. You met with them before that on July 1, 1998. You met with them --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995 you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You met with them on February 4, 1998. You met with them on July 1, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said 1995 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. You met with them on October 21, 1999. You met with them on 12 March 2001. On any of those occasions -- during any of those occasions were you truthful about the knowledge in your own participation about the events in Srebrenica, yes or no? Did you disclose, I know about the massacres, I know what happened? Did you ever say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not tell the entire truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say you did not tell the entire truth, let's not quibble over semantics. You were giving false information, right? Half a truth is equal to half a lie, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can call it the way you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go on to this statement, because we're using this as the context for what happens later. You were asked specifically if you observed male population being separated from the female population. And you say, and I'm going to -- I'll read the answer and then we're going to talk about it: "They had some access in one convoy because the military police tried to separate some people they recognised. One representative of local parliament of Srebrenica. We did not have enough force to stop separation. The commander of the army refused. He with some others were in the hands of the army. For this single person, I know he was exchanged for a Serb commander, who was in the hands of the Muslims. As far as I know, one of these -- for others you have to check with the army." Then you go and state: "On my intervention and the intervention of UNPROFOR, after that such things didn't happen. UNPROFOR said they wouldn't participate in the evacuation if that happened. The destiny of the other people is unknown to me. You will have to ask the army. It was a small number of people." Mr. Deronjic, were you being truthful when you said that you had an -- that you intervened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say that you intervened, with whom did you intervene?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in the interview, in the last interview, you can find it there, then the information had been conveyed to me by Vasic. I wanted him to go and fetch Mladic and tell him not to do that. In the meantime, and you have just reminded me of this. From the UNPROFOR headquarters I received a phone call in my office, they told me that separations were taking place. And this is exactly what they said, they intervened -- and actually they wanted me to intervene. And I told Vasic, Mr. Vasic, please go and find Mladic. Because I myself did not go to Potocari. Go find Mr. Mladic and tell him not to do that, which you can find in my last statement, in my last transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given your position as the president of the SDS, you had access to a vehicle, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact you even had a driver, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I did. However, during the war I did not have a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, you had a driver. We're talking about those days. Work with me, on those days?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And given your position, you had access to gasoline to put in the car, should you wish to go someplace. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Bratunac to Potocari is approximately 5 kilometres, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you heard that this incident was going on, the incidents that men were being separated indiscriminately from their loved ones, you never made an effort to do anything about it, other than, according to you, tell Vasic, who was from Zvornik, to talk to Mladic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yet, according to your mandate, pursuant to you being appointed by the president, you were responsible for all civilian -- for all the civilians there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that included also the men that were of military age. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from those in respect of whom our services had information that they had committed crimes. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would agree with you that there was -- a wish had been expressed that those war criminals known should be separated to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's not that a wish had been expressed. It was an order issued by the president, an order that I conveyed to the meeting at Fontana. It was not anybody's wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. So in other words, you were ordered. And then, given your mandate, you were supposed to be ordering. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supposed to convey this information to the meeting at Fontana. Those were orders issued by Karadzic and not by myself. You're deliberately altering the semantics, and then you get angry with me for providing additional comments. You said yourself that we should not play games. I am fully aware of these issues. I know the problems. Please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So based on that, am I to conclude that you were merely a conduit, like somebody on -- doing duty. You know, he was somebody who was just there to pass a message, like a duty officer. He's just passing the message. Somebody's saying, do this, and then just passing on the message. Is that how you were?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can draw any conclusion that you want. I was precise in my description as to what I did. You may draw any conclusion that you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Later on on that page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. I got lost in my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to conclude, Mr. Deronjic, this first statement that you gave. At the end of page 4 in your version you state here -- or it's rather unclear, but I believe it's your statement that in fact: "Before the fall of Srebrenica they," that is the Muslims, "had a 24-hour guarantee by Mladic for those not fighting would be allowed to leave freely, but only a small number of Muslims of Muslim military accepted this proposal." According to this document, this is what you told Mr. Ralston back on 16th December, 1997. Did you, in fact, make that statement, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you referring to the same document? What page, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 4, last paragraph -- it should be paragraph 11 by our count, on that page.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find it, but I believe that those are my true words. I do not wish to waste too much time looking for it, but it's true that I stated that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was that -- was that an accurate statement, that Mladic had given a 24-hour guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is an accurate statement. At the meeting held at Fontana on the 12th. This is what he offered to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think we established yesterday that you were not at that meeting when that was offered?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was present. We're talking about the 12th. This is what he presented to the Muslims on the 12th at the meeting which I attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would have been around the noon of the -- midday on the 12th. That was the only meeting that you attended and it's your recollection that's when Mladic made that offer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only meeting of that kind, yes. And it was at that time that Mladic made that offer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you had an opportunity to review or to view the video that was prepared of that meeting? I believe there is some video footage of that, is there not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've been told that there is a video footage. I have not had an opportunity to see it, but I did see portions of the transcript from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Portions of the transcript of the meeting. I'm a little confused now. Was somebody taking minutes of that meeting, notes, and then formulated a transcript as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the transcript of the video footage of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that provided to you as part of the disclosure material, or was that information that you gathered through your sources, be they at the Detention Unit, from other detainees, or in the field as you were doing your own investigation trying figure out what really happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never in possession of that document, nor did I find it as part of any investigation. I was merely shown the document, not long ago, actually, two or three days ago, as part of the disclosure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown by the Office of the Prosecution or by --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, I wanted to know whether such a document existed. I wanted to know what exists on paper to that effect, and the Prosecutor provided me with this material. I just wanted to check whether I was correct in my interpretation of what was said at the meeting. This, like I said, took place two or three days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's rather interesting. I read the proofing notes. I don't see - and I might be wrong, I might have missed it - anywhere where it states that this was provided to you by the Office of the Prosecution for you to review. Was that -- I could be wrong, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it's in there. If he doesn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll take a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll accept Mr. McCloskey's word for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, if we could move on to the next statement that you gave, this was on February 4, 1998. This was approximately three months after your first encounter with someone from the Office of the Prosecution. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three months after your initial meeting with someone from the Office of the Prosecution, you had your second meeting, this time with Mr. Ruez. Correct? And for the record, I'm referring to D93 --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. February the 4th, 1998. Yes, I've just got the transcript of the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at that point in time -- by that point in time, you had -- you were aware of the areas in which the Office of the Prosecution were interested in with respect to you, that is. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially correct. I was aware of the main topics that were to be discussed -- that had already been discussed, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And in fact, the main topic was Srebrenica, not Glogova, for which you were ultimately indicted for. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this particular interview, the following one, the main topic was Srebrenica. But I have to say in the practice of the Tribunal and their investigation teams, there is no procedure whereby I would have been informed in advance about what would be discussed. So the issue of Glogova could have also been included and everything else that was interesting for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. But by this point in time you had three months at least to gather your thoughts and prepare yourself, at least mentally, for the interview with Mr. Ruez. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Three months had gone by between those meetings; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ruez did not show up unannounced. You were informed in advance of when he would be coming to have an interview with you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But that does not leave much room. You usually get about five or six days prior to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, Mr. Ruez began the interview by informing you - and this is on page 1 of the English transcript, and it's also on page 1, line 14 to 15, in the Srpski version - that your statement would be recorded and, I quote, "might eventually be used as evidence during the proceedings at The Hague Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- so at least at the beginning of that particular interview, which is your second encounter, you knew for a fact that what you were saying would eventually or could eventually be used in a legal proceeding. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You can see that I said "proceedings against whom," but I was a little surprised. But I understood what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And I would suspect that you also understood the importance of being truthful, honest, and complete in your answers, now that you had been forewarned by Mr. Ruez that anything you had said, even though you were still under the title of witness, might be used in a legal proceeding. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the interview begins by you describing your various positions in your background in politics. That's on the second page, but we will skip that because we're going to deal with it later on, if that's okay with you. So we're rather focused now -- our attention on page 3, and we're going to go back to some of the information that we've already covered. On this occasion, and I'm reading -- in your version it would be page 3, lines 14 all the way into page 4, line 4. In the English version, it begins at line 22, page 3. You say: "I have learned about a decision taken by President Karadzic through the mass media. Some of my friends heard that news on the radio and they told me about it. At that very moment, I was staying at the front line, together with the soldiers. I asked permission to leave and to go to the command in order to get in contact" --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. It does not say -- it does not say: "I asked permission," but it just said: "I decided to go to the command. Who should I ask the permission from."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me read the English version and then we will see. It states here: "I asked permission to leave and to go to the command in order to get in contact with President Karadzic and we had a telephone conversation." Now, I don't know whether there's a mistranslation, but it's fair to say that you didn't need to ask anyone for permission because you were the highest authority in Bratunac at that time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct. Allow me to go back to something that you keep repeating; it's an assertion. It's very important. Please allow me -- it's very important for me to explain this to you. You, sir, you keep using an assertion, and I am patiently waiting for the moment to respond with my counter arguments. You're suggesting my power, you're attaching important to the function I was carrying out at the time in Bratunac. I will be very brief and I really do not want to be malicious in the least at this point. You are an educated man, and we know we can discuss the phenomenon of power until tomorrow. You know that it is the subject of various scientific research, so let's not talk about it. There are serious studies about this phenomenon. Please allow me to explain. Allow me to explain. You are saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, give the opportunity to the witness to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, I merely wanted to say in the next segment we will be covering his background in the greatest of details, specifically as to his powers. Now, I don't mind the explanation, we're just going to have to do it again all over later. So we will get to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I absolutely agree, I would just like to have this opportunity. I'm patiently waiting for such an opportunity. I'm just afraid that I will not be given the chance, but please continue. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will cover it. I have a whole line of questions on that. In any event, based on this particular statement that I just read, it would appear that you had to ask permission. Now, you were questioned by Mr. Milosevic not too long ago. Do you recall that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I remember that he questioned me. I don't remember each detail. I didn't have the opportunity to look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have the official transcript here, and I want to quote the question and answer. And this can be found on page 29.682 -- no, 29.682. So that's 29.682. This was on Wednesday, 26 November 2003. And I'm reading from line 19 where Mr. Milosevic asks you: "You say that Vidoje Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade, ordered to you to go into Srebrenica. That is in paragraph 184 - on the 11th of July." And incidentally I'm told for the record this should be marked as P692 or this is marked as P692 for identification. And your answer to that question was: "Yes." Now, we'll get to paragraph 184 of your statement. But from this answer, it would appear that you're suggesting that Mr. Blagojevic ordered you to go into Srebrenica. And since this is part of the record that's coming in, all these documents, I would like a clear answer. The fact is Mr. Blagojevic never ordered you to go into Srebrenica; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, please, if you have this version in Serbian, then I would like it to read it in the context. I'm not sure whether the translation is correct or whether what you're reading is quite correct. So if I may be given the opportunity to look at the transcript in Serbian and I will reply, just to be sure whether everything is as it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regretfully the Tribunal, for whatever reason, doesn't do a Serbian version of the proceedings. We have the English version, so this is from the actual transcript. Now, I do -- I can provide you with paragraph 198 [sic] of your statement, but the question that Mr. Milosevic posed to you, and I'll read it in context. You say that: "Vidoje Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade, ordered to you to go into Srebrenica - that is in paragraph 184 - on the 11th of July. "A. Yes. "Q. But you found out on your way to Srebrenica that Karadzic was looking for you? "A. Yes. "Q. That's why you didn't go into Srebrenica, you returned to Bratunac instead? "A. Yes." Now, if we -- that was your answer, your answer was, yes, Vidoje Blagojevic ordered you. So we have a clear understanding.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't comment on that. I'm not sure whether the interpretation is correct or perhaps I did not understand Mr. Milosevic's question very well. It's possible that there's a mistake there. In the transcript -- I mean in my interview to the Prosecution, I described that encounter on the 11th as just a chance encounter with Mr. Blagojevic. And I said that I had heard from him that there was an order to enter Srebrenica, not that he had ordered me. That is not true at all. And perhaps if I had understood Milosevic's question wrongly, I would like to correct myself. It's possible that there's also a mistake in the interpretation. Perhaps we can establish that at some other time. So I did meet with Mr. Blagojevic, just by chance, during the entry to Srebrenica in the area of Pribicevac. And he said that there was an order issued to enter Srebrenica, but this order did not refer to me. And the time I was not a member of his units. We just briefly commented on that and set out practically together towards Srebrenica. That is the correct answer. I really don't know how this came about. Perhaps I had made a mistake in relation to Milosevic's question, or perhaps it's a translation mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I wanted to clarify that, because in paragraph 19 -- 184 of the -- of your statement called Witness Statement, it's dated the 26th of November, 2003, you do state, in fact, that: "Vidoje Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade, was there and advised us that the order had been given to enter Srebrenica." So I just wanted to clarify that, that at no point in time Mr. Blagojevic had ordered you to --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think this is a very important piece of the evidence, but I believe that the witness and you have some disputes concerning with the translation of that paragraph. So in this way I would like to ask the Registrar to inform the translation unit to check both the English and the B/C/S translations in the Milosevic case on that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. And for the record, I believe I was just quoting from what has been marked as P693.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We clarified that issue. Now, if we were to go further down on that same page, you state: "Since it was already the nighttime when I learned about this, I've asked him to meet," meaning Karadzic, "I've asked him to meet me in the course of the following day so I can get some closer instructions in relation to my new function and my new obligations. In the course of the following day, I had a meeting with Mr. Karadzic in the building of the Presidency in Pale." And then you go on to explain what had occurred, you know, the instructions that you were given, which we've already talked about. So here it seems that you're stating that you did not, in fact, go to Pale on the 11th, but rather in the course of the following day.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We explained yesterday that there was a confusion about the dates and that this is not correct. I said that. I did not go the next day either, but in later checks I determined that I actually went on the 14th. I can describe to you exactly how I came to this information that I was at Pale on the 14th. So if you're interested, I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to get to the 14th, because that relates to the events of the 13th. But if you did not go to Pale on the 11th, then you must have been in Bratunac on the 11th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th I was at Pribicevac; that is correct. On the 11th in the afternoon, I found out that I had been appointed to some function in Srebrenica. On the 11th in the evening, I was at the command and I spoke with Karadzic. This is the correct information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the command post is located in Bratunac, in the city of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade command was in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so you would have been in Bratunac that evening, afternoon and evening. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your office, the office that is of the party of the SDS, was also in Bratunac, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it was in the centre, in the heart, of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is in the centre there, because there is nothing beyond that. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. And the Hotel Fontana is also in the centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long would it take you to go from your office to the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten -- five minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five minutes. And I take it your office, being the president of such an important party, probably had windows?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could look out, see what's going on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see at the Fontana -- I mean, there is no -- it's not possible -- there was no view out on that part of the street, but you could see on to the street, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question wasn't whether you could see the Hotel Fontana, my question was whether you could look out and see. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on that particular evening -- afternoon/evening, there were two meetings in the Hotel Fontana. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I have some information about that, but I don't know how much and with whom these meetings on the 11th in the evening were held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you if you knew back then; I'm asking you if you know now. We'll get to what you knew back then.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems like I had the opportunity to see later. It was determined unequivocally that there were meetings at the Fontana on the 11th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And during that period of time you had Mladic in Bratunac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And his fairly large and quite visible entourage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also had General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that really. I did see him at Pribicevac, but I don't know whether he was in Bratunac at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time, he was nonetheless - as far as you knew - the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information is unclear. To this day it's not clear to me whether he was de facto or de jure replaced and when Krstic was appointed. But it's clear to me that he was at this important post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about de jure, because in that we can see with some clarity that we don't have a decision from Karadzic until, I believe, it's the 12th or the 13th. But on this particular day, on the 11th, he's still the commander, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's inaccurate. The order from Karadzic was not on those days, just to clear up the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was actually later, but that's fine. I'm giving him some leeway. I'm erring on the side of caution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was, right? Now, also there was General Krstic. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had no information about whether they were in Bratunac or not. Both of the people we are talking about, I knew they were at Pribicevac. I saw Zivanovic only at one point, to be more precise, and Mr. Krstic was at Pribicevac. Whether on the 12th or the 11th in the evening he was at Bratunac, I didn't have any information to that effect at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Mr. Deronjic, that on that particular afternoon and evening, Bratunac was swarming with members of the VRS, and I'm talking about VIP members, officers from the Main Staff, officers from the Drina Corps? And they were quite visible.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were at certain points in time. Of course I know -- I know today precisely that they were all there somewhere nearby, but whether that afternoon or that evening and at what time they were in Srebrenica, you know that Mladic entered Srebrenica. I assume that a certain number of officers were with him in Srebrenica, that they had some sort of speech up there, that this was taped, that there was some kind of ceremony conducted up there. I assume that they spent some time at the UNPROFOR base. At what time they came to Bratunac, entered the Fontana, left the Fontana, that I don't know because it's not possible to see from my office because the building on the side is completely shielded and the entrance to the Fontana, to the parking, is from a side street which is not visible at all from my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while all of this was going on in Bratunac - and I might add, it was quite a festive occasion, the fall of Srebrenica - you were holed up in your office, totally secluded from what was going on in this town which you described as small, and almost the entire town is the centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. I was in my office. The rest of the evening I spent in my office, not alone of course, but in the presence of my close associates from the municipality, including some people from the police. I cannot remember exactly who was there in my office on that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it had you known, had you known that Mladic was going to be meeting with representatives of UNPROFOR and then later on with representatives from both UNPROFOR and the Muslim community that was in Potocari, you as president of the SDS would have at least made a cameo visit, presence, in those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not. I would not have appeared unless Mladic invited me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you already had spoken to Karadzic and you already knew your function and you already knew that based on the orders from the president, who was also the supreme commander of the VRS at the same time, that part of your duties, part of your mandate, was the security and well being of all of those that were in Potocari. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
